name: Hana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the billing line for Northvale Energy, the regional gas and power supplier, at their contact centre on the ring road. I log in at eight, put my headset on, and it's back-to-back calls about bills, meter readings and payment plans until the lunch break at twelve-thirty. The bit I like is when someone rings in crying about a bill they can't pay and I can set them up on a plan they can actually manage. What wears me out is the timer on the screen telling me the call's gone past six minutes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years this spring. I live with my partner Jonas, he drives the number 14 bus, and we rent a two-bed flat above a bakery. We've got about three months of bills put by, which took us ages. I don't use any of the AI stuff, not even the reply suggestions they put in the chat window last year. I just switch that box off and type my own answers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds about right to me. The chat box they gave us mostly suggests the wrong answer anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, mostly to my team in the break room. We've had three years of managers promising the robots will do the boring bits and it's all been a bit of a flop. Online I'd probably share something from the union about bosses using AI as an excuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but I wouldn't relax. Northvale already moved half the payment calls to an automated phone menu, and they'd keep chipping at us even if the AI is rubbish. My worry was never really the technology, it's management looking for any reason to cut heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it now, no changes there. I'd keep putting forty a month into our savings pot and go to the union branch meetings on the first Tuesday. If they push another self-service tool, I'd want the union to get a say in it before it lands on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit tired. It's the same grind, the same targets, the same six-minute timer. Nothing to panic about, but nothing to look forward to either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management would keep chipping away even if the AI is rubbish. What does chipping away look like on your floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year they didn't replace two people who left, so the queue just got longer for the rest of us. Now there's always a red number on the wall board showing who's waiting. Even with useless AI, a manager can still decide fewer of us is fine and let the customers wait longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your hours or pay did get squeezed, what would go first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The little holiday we do every August would go first, the week at Jonas's aunt's caravan. After that it's takeaways and my gym membership. Rent's the one thing we can't touch, the landlord put it up again in June.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** fell flat, like I always said it would.
I'd share **union posts** warning that bosses still use AI as an excuse to cut.
think: I'd feel **relieved** about the tech, but not about management.
Northvale can still **leave posts empty** and let the queue grow, AI or no AI.
do: Keep doing calls the **same way**, with the reply-suggestion box switched off.
Keep saving **forty a month** and attend union branch meetings every first Tuesday.
feel: She feels **tired** rather than scared; it's the same grind and targets.
S0.quote: Even with useless AI, a manager can still decide fewer of us is fine and let the customers wait longer.
fieldNote: She points her worry at **management**, not at the technology itself.
Unfilled posts and a **longer queue** already shape her days before any AI arrives.
Rent rising in June means the **cushion** feels smaller than three months.

steps.text: Keep taking billing calls with the AI suggestion box switched off
Put forty a month into the joint savings pot with Jonas
Attend the union branch meeting every first Tuesday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's not a picture, that's just next year at Northvale. Answering customers is right there in the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union at the table now, not after the fact. Online I'd be the one posting that companies should have to keep a human on the line by law. I'd say it loud, because if nobody says it, the board just does whatever saves money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is the exact thing they'll shrink first. A bot can tell you your balance and set up a payment plan, even if it does it badly. People like me, who are fine but not the best on the floor, are the ones they let go in the second round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up as a union rep the month it started, because someone has to read the redundancy terms. I'd push our savings from forty to a hundred a month and cancel the August caravan week. I'd also start looking at the hospital switchboard and the council housing office, because those jobs feel like they'd keep a person on the phone longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes my stomach drop a bit. I'm not good with new systems and I know it. I'd be angry more than scared, but the scared bit would be there at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good with new systems. If Northvale asked you to supervise the bots instead of taking calls, would you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, because I'd have to, but I'd hate it. Watching a screen of bot chats and stepping in when one goes wrong isn't why I do this job. My friend Bea tried the pilot last spring and said it felt like cleaning up after someone else all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray, who sits next to me, is fifty-eight and can barely use the new CRM. If they cut the floor in half, he's out, and nobody hires a fifty-eight-year-old call handler. I'd worry about him more than me, if I'm honest.

say: I'd say the **union** needs to be at the table before the cuts, not after.
I'd post that **a human** on the line should be required by law.
think: My job is the **first to shrink**, because a bot can set up a payment plan.
Average performers like me go in the **second round** of cuts.
do: Become a **union rep** the first month to read the redundancy terms.
Raise savings to **a hundred a month** and cancel the August caravan week.
Look at **hospital switchboard** and council housing office jobs as a fallback.
feel: She feels **angry** first, with fear underneath that shows up at night.
S1.quote: A bot can tell you your balance and set up a payment plan, even if it does it badly.
fieldNote: She sees her own billing work as **directly in line** for automation.
Her plan is about **protection**, through the union and savings, not about learning AI.
She worries for her older colleague Ray **more than herself**, which says a lot about her.

steps.text: Sign up as a union rep at the Northvale contact centre
Raise monthly savings from forty to a hundred
Cancel the August week at the caravan
Apply for hospital switchboard and council housing office jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our lease even runs out. I don't know what you do with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a choice rich people made, not weather that just happened to us. I'd be at every rally and I'd be posting that the government has to step in with a basic income or a jobs guarantee. At work I'd say don't sign anything without the union reading it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone in two years, maybe less. All of it is talking and typing, there's no hands-on part to hide in. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me, it just tells me where everyone else will run to first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food from day one and try to get our pot to six months. I'd look into an apprenticeship that uses my hands, maybe care work at the home where my mum used to work, because those jobs last three years longer. And I'd be at the union every week pushing for proper redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor's tilting. I'd be lying awake running numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on work lasts three years longer. Would three years in care work actually help you, or just delay things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd buy time for the politics to catch up, that's how I'd see it. Three years of wages while the government works out what to do with everyone is better than three years on the dole. I'm not stupid about it, I know the robots come for care homes too, but people would fight harder to keep a human by their gran's bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not having a wedding next year, we're having a savings account. He'd laugh, because he always does when I go serious. Then I'd ask him how long he thinks bus drivers have, because his job's the hands-on one and that's our three years.

say: I'd say AGI is **a choice** made by rich people, not bad weather.
I'd demand a **basic income** or jobs guarantee at rallies and online.
think: My job is **all talking and typing**, so it's gone within two years.
Robots arriving later only shows where **everyone else** will run first.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and aim for six months saved.
Look for a **care work** apprenticeship at the home where her mum worked.
Push the union **every week** for proper redundancy pay.
feel: She feels **sick**, like the floor is tilting, and expects sleepless nights.
S2.quote: Three years of wages while the government works out what to do with everyone is better than three years on the dole.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** before robots as time for politics to catch up.
Jonas's bus job is the **household's buffer**, since his work is hands-on.
She'd postpone a **possible wedding** to protect savings.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent and food from the first month
Apply for a care work apprenticeship at the local care home
Push the union weekly for better redundancy pay
Go to rallies for a basic income or jobs guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still fast for someone like me. But at least you'd see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to plan. I'd be pushing the union to negotiate retraining money now, while companies still need us. Online I'd keep it practical: here's what to ask your employer this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just enough time for me to waste it. I know myself, I'd keep doing my calls and telling myself I'll sort it next year. The desk part of my job goes in 2031 either way, there's nothing to wait for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the union to win a training fund, then I'd actually use it, probably for a care certificate at the college on Mill Lane. I'd keep my Northvale job while I study at night, because the money matters. We'd save the August holiday money every year until we hit six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy most days and scared some nights. It's less of a punch than the two-year one. But it still feels like a clock on the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you know you'd waste the time. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having Bea start with me. If my friend's signed up for the same evening class, I'll go, because I won't let her sit there alone. On my own I'd find a reason every week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots coming three years after AGI, in 2034. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means care work isn't forever, I know that. But by 2034 I'd be thirty-five, and I'd rather be thirty-five with a trade than thirty-five with a dead headset. Maybe by then there'd be rules about people looking after people.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for the government not to plan.
I'd push the union to win **retraining money** while firms still need staff.
think: I'd probably **waste the time** by putting things off year after year.
The desk part of my job **goes in 2031** whatever I do.
do: Use a union-won fund for a **care certificate** at the Mill Lane college.
Keep the **Northvale job** while studying in the evenings.
Save the **August holiday money** each year until six months is covered.
feel: She feels **uneasy** most days and scared on some nights.
S3.quote: I'd rather be thirty-five with a trade than thirty-five with a dead headset.
fieldNote: She's honest that she'd **procrastinate** without someone beside her.
Her friend Bea is her **real motivator** for retraining.
She hopes **rules** will protect human care work by 2034.

steps.text: Take an evening care certificate at the Mill Lane college with Bea
Push the union to negotiate a training fund this year
Bank the August holiday money until savings reach six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds like forever, which is exactly the problem. Everyone will say there's loads of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the chance to do this properly, with the workers in the room. I'd keep saying it at union meetings and online until people got sick of me. I'd also say the companies should pay for the retraining, not us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd relax for the first few years, I know I would. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, which is young enough to start again. But I'd always have that thought in the back of my head while I'm on a call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep going to the union meetings. Somewhere around year three I'd start a part-time course, maybe nursing support or care. Jonas and I might even go ahead with the wedding and a deposit, because ten years is long enough to plan a life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. It's like knowing the landlord will sell in ten years. You can live with it, but you never quite feel at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might go ahead with the wedding and a deposit. Wouldn't that tie you down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I can't put my whole life on hold for a decade. If we buy, it'd be somewhere cheap near the hospital, so either of us could get work there later. Jonas would laugh at me for planning a house around a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly even with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government and the big companies, the same as always. Ten years is plenty of time to set up retraining and rules, so if the government wastes it, that's on them. It's not on people like Ray who just did their jobs.

say: I'd say ten years is the **chance to plan** with workers in the room.
I'd insist **companies pay** for retraining, not workers.
think: I'd probably **relax** for the first few years and know it.
At thirty-seven I'd still be **young enough** to start again.
do: Keep the job and keep attending **union meetings** every month.
Start a **part-time course** in care or nursing support around year three.
Plan the **wedding and a deposit** on a cheap place near the hospital.
feel: She feels **calmer but not calm**, like living with a landlord who'll sell.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty of time to set up retraining and rules, so if the government wastes it, that's on them.
fieldNote: She wants to **live her life** rather than pause it for a decade.
Her blame sits firmly with **government and big companies**.
Buying near the **hospital** is her quiet hedge for later work.

steps.text: Keep the Northvale billing job and attend monthly union meetings
Start a part-time care course around the third year
Plan the wedding and save for a flat near the hospital
Press the union to make employers fund retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. There's no time to retrain and my job is all talking. What would help is proper redundancy pay and a government that pays for people to train into care and hospital work while they still have a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people on the other end of the line. Half my calls are old people who can't work an app and are scared of a bill. If the bots take over, I'm not the only one who loses something.

headlineQuote: Half my calls are old people who can't work an app and are scared of a bill.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** billing agent at Northvale Energy's contact centre, six years in.
She lives with partner **Jonas**, a bus driver, and they have about **three months** saved.
She refuses to use **AI tools** and blames management, not technology, for cuts.
Her answer to every scenario runs through the **union**, savings and a fallback into care work.
She only gets **calmer** when there's ten years to plan, and still not fully calm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job is all talking and there's no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Proper **redundancy pay** and government-funded training into care and hospital work while still earning.
